passages.original: Ipse autem Tacitus imperator primam talem ad Probum epistulam dedit: Tacitus Augustus Probo, me quidem senatus principem fecit de prudentis exercitus voluntate, attamen sciendum tibi est tuis nunc umeris magis incubuisse rem publicam, qui et quantus sis omnes novimus, scit senatus, adesto igitur nostris necessitatibus, tuae familiae adsere, ut soles, rem publicam, nos tibi decreto totius orientis ducatu salarium quinquiplex fecimus, ornamenta militaria geminavimus, consulatum in annum proximum nobiscum decrevimus ; te enim manet pro virtutibus tuis Capitolina palmata. Ferunt quidam Probo id pro imperii omine fuisse, quod Tacitus scripsit, Te manet Capitolina palmata. sed in hanc sententiam omnibus semper consulibus scribebatur.
passages.english: Now Tacitus himself, as emperor, sent his first letter to Probus as follows: "Tacitus Augustus to Probus. The senate has indeed made me emperor, in accordance with the wish of the prudent army; yet you must know that the commonwealth now rests more heavily on your shoulders. We all know who and how great you are; the senate knows it. Stand by us, then, in our needs; claim the commonwealth for your household, as you are accustomed to do. We, by decree granting you the command of the whole East, have made your salary fivefold, have doubled your military decorations, and have decreed the consulship for the coming year together with us; for the *palmata* of the Capitol awaits you for your merits." Some say that it was an omen of empire for Probus that Tacitus wrote, "The *palmata* of the Capitol awaits you." But this was always written in these terms to all consuls.
passages.notes: *palmata* (Capitolina palmata): the palm-embroidered triumphal/consular robe (tunica palmata), worn in the procession to the Capitol. "Prudentis exercitus" may be corrupt (some read "prudentissimi"). "Tuae familiae adsere ... rem publicam" is obscure; the sense may be "defend the state as you do your own household," and the text may be corrupt.
